summary.value: The authors propose GUI-KV, a smart and efficient KV-cache compression framework for GUI agents that deal with tons of screenshots and long tasks. Instead of retraining the models, GUI-KV just plugs into existing agents and makes them faster and lighter by pruning redundant cache states. The key idea is that GUI screenshots are full of repetitive visuals, so the paper introduces a spatio-temporal theorem-guided method: (1) spatial saliency guidance, which scores tokens based on their L2-norm (how much “information energy” they carry) and attention weights; and (2) temporal redundancy scoring, which uses QR decomposition to detect overlapping key subspaces between frames and drop repetitive tokens. This simple yet well-reasoned design leads to large speedups and even slight accuracy gains over full-cache models.

strengths.value:
The paper  builds an argument from the observation (Fig. 1, lines 108–215 and 162–215) that GUI attention sparsity is uniformly above 0.99 across all layers. This leads to a clean, theory-backed conclusion that uniform budget allocation is optimal for GUI workloads, overturning prior assumptions from methods like PyramidKV and VL-Cache that rely on varying per-layer budgets.

he proposed saliency + redundancy scoring (lines 270–323) ties practical algorithmic components to theoretical motivation. It’s easy to implement, works plug-and-play without retraining.

weaknesses.value:
The core theorem and sparsity analysis (lines 162–215) hinge on an assumption of uniform high attention sparsity (> 0.99). This is empirically true for GUI screenshots but might not hold for other multimodal agents (e.g., video or natural-scene reasoning). The paper doesn’t clarify how GUI-KV behaves when this uniformity breaks down.

The temporal redundancy mechanism (lines 270–323) assumes low-rank subspaces (r ≪ dₕ), but the computational overhead of repeated QR per frame could become significant in real-time agents or larger contexts. While the authors mention negligible prefill cost (lines 432–485), no timing breakdown is provided for larger r or more screenshots.

Although the authors reason that uniform budget allocation is “optimal,” there is no formal proof or convergence guarantee. The argument is empirical rather than mathematical, so the claimed “theorem-like” property is more observational than theoretically rigorous.

Minor weakness: (1) Some parameter choices (e.g., α = 0.5, τ = 0.1 in Eq. 5) are not justified. (2) The interaction between spatial and temporal modules isn’t theoretically characterized (just shown empirically in Fig. 4).

summary.value:
This paper addresses the computational inefficiency of GUI agents when processing long sequences of high-resolution screenshots by proposing GUI-KV, a plug-and-play, training-free key-value cache compression method tailored for GUI environments. The authors first conduct a thorough empirical analysis and reveal a key insight: unlike natural images, GUI screenshots exhibit uniformly high attention sparsity across all transformer layers. This finding invalidates existing layer-wise adaptive budget allocation strategies, which rely on inter-layer sparsity variation and thus misallocate cache in GUI contexts. Consequently, the authors advocate for a simple yet effective uniform budget allocation across layers.
Building on this, GUI-KV introduces two novel components: (1) spatial saliency guidance, which augments attention scores with the L2 norm of visual token hidden states to better preserve semantically important regions; and (2) temporal redundancy scoring, which uses QR decomposition to project historical keys onto the current frame’s key subspace and preferentially prune tokens that are redundant over time. Extensive experiments across six established GUI agent benchmarks—including visual grounding, offline action prediction, and online evaluation—demonstrate that GUI-KV consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it recovers near-full-cache accuracy with only 10–20% cache budget, and in some cases, it improves step accuracy by +4.1% while reducing decoding FLOPs by 38.9% compared to the full-cache baseline. Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of the spatial and temporal components.
The paper is well-motivated, technically sound, and empirically rigorous. The proposed method is simple, effective, and directly applicable to real-world deployment of efficient GUI agents. The writing is clear, and the analysis is insightful. This work makes a valuable contribution to efficient multimodal inference and is suitable for publication at ICLR.

strengths.value:
（1）	The paper addresses a critical efficiency bottleneck in GUI agents, KV cache explosion when processing long sequences of high-resolution screenshots, a key barrier to real-world deployment.

（2）	The authors conduct the first systematic analysis showing that GUI screenshots exhibit uniformly extreme attention sparsity across all transformer layers, in stark contrast to natural images. This invalidates layer-wise adaptive budgeting strategies used in prior KV compression methods.

（3）	Clear presentation and strong reproducibility: The method is well-described, with pseudocode, hyperparameter details, and thorough ablations provided in the appendix, ensuring transparency and ease of replication.

weaknesses.value:
（1）All experiments use pre-recorded screenshots from benchmarks like ScreenSpot and AgentNetBench. However, real-world GUIs often contain dynamic components that violate the assumption of high temporal redundancy, potentially undermining the QR-based subspace projection.

（2）The paper reports aggregate accuracy gains but provides no error case studies. For instance: in which tasks does GUI-KV underperform? Are failures caused by premature pruning of small but critical UI elements? Such analysis is essential to delineate the method’s failure modes.

（3）The paper includes insufficient visualizations, which limits the reader’s ability to fully grasp the core mechanisms and empirical findings of the proposed method. The authors are encouraged to include additional illustrative figures or case studies to improve clarity and strengthen the presentation.

> Q2: Sensitivity of r.

We thank the reviewer for this question. We had already investigated this exact question in Appendix B.2 and reported the results in Table 4.Our empirical results demonstrate that GUI-KV is remarkably robust to the choice of rank $r$. As shown in Table 4, varying $r$ from 8 to 128 yields consistently strong performance, with all settings outperforming the baselines reported in Table 12. While we found $r=32$ to be the optimal sweet spot, even a very low rank ($r=8$) maintains high accuracy (e.g., 21.7 at 80% budget). Regarding the suggestion of an adaptive $r$ per layer: While theoretically interesting, we believe it is practically unnecessary due to the negligible cost of the operation. As detailed in Table 3 (Appendix B.1), the QR decomposition accounts for only ~0.28% of the attention scoring compute cost (0.013 GFLOPs vs 4.607 GFLOPs). Since the computational overhead is already vanishingly small with a fixed $r$, introducing an adaptive mechanism would add implementation complexity without yielding meaningful efficiency gains.

> Q3: Use of Different Evaluation Metrics 

We thank the reviewer for this question. We would like to respectfully clarify that we did not introduce any new metrics in this paper.

The use of different metrics is a direct consequence of adhering to the standard, established evaluation protocols for each respective benchmark, as defined by their original authors. The field uses different metrics because the tasks themselves are different; for example, "click accuracy" is the standard for single-step visual grounding (like ScreenSpot-V2) , while "success rate" is the standard for complex, multi-step online tasks (like OSWorld-Verified). Using a single, unified metric across these functionally distinct tasks would not be appropriate or meaningful.


Our goal was to ensure our results are directly comparable to prior and future work. As we state in Section 4.1, we follow the same evaluation settings as UGround. This adherence to established community standards is a necessary practice for proper evaluation.

> Q5: Identical Performance at 100% Budget

We would like to clarify that this identical performance is indeed expected and mathematically necessary.

In the context of KV cache compression, a 100% budget definitionally means that all KV states are retained in the cache. Regardless of the ranking policy used (whether it is SnapKV, PyramidKV, or GUI-KV), if the budget allows for 100% retention, every method effectively selects the complete set of tokens. Consequently, the underlying model performs standard attention over the full history in all cases. Since the input to the attention mechanism is identical (the full cache), the output and resulting performance must be identical.

> W3: Latency Cost During the Decoding Phase

We thank the reviewer for raising this concern, as it allows us to clarify a critical point about our method's efficiency.

The reviewer's concern about re-evaluation during the decoding phase stems from a misunderstanding. Our entire scoring and compression pipeline, including both spatial saliency and temporal redundancy scoring, is executed __only one time, during the prefill phase__.

This single, one-off computation operates on the initial prompt (the screenshots and text instruction) to create a static, compressed KV cache before any auto-regressive generation begins. This focus on a single, prefill-phase compression step is the __standard setup employed in most recent KV cache literature__, including our baselines SnapKV, VL-Cache, and PyramidKV. We additionally demonstrate in Section 5.3 and Appendix B.1 that the overhead of this prefill step is negligible .


During the subsequent auto-regressive decoding phase, no further scoring, pruning, or re-evaluation occurs. Like a standard Transformer, we simply append the new KV pairs from each generated token to this already compressed cache. This is a convention of 

Therefore, the additional latency cost of our method during the decoding phase is zero. On the contrary, by creating a significantly smaller cache, our method reduces the computational cost of every decoding step, which is the primary source of our efficiency gains (e.g., the 38.9% MFLOPs reduction shown in Table 2).

> Q6: Hyperparameter Sensitivity and Robustness

As we already discussed in __Appendix C__, we determined these values (\alpha=2, \tau=3.5) based on a small-scale preliminary validation on a subset of the ScreenSpot-V2 training split, aiming to balance the contribution of attention scores and spatial saliency. Once selected, we __fixed these values and applied them unchanged across all subsequent experiments__. We believe the strongest evidence for their robustness is the method's __consistent performance across the paper's diverse experimental landscape__. We used this identical configuration for: two distinct model architectures (UI-TARS-1.5-7B and OpenCUA-7B) and six disparate benchmarks ranging from static visual grounding (ScreenSpot) to dynamic OS interaction (OSWorld-Verified) and mobile control (AndroidControl). The fact that GUI-KV consistently outperforms baselines on such varied tasks without requiring per-task or per-model hyperparameter tuning demonstrates that the chosen settings are robust and generalizable, rather than specifically-tuned to a specific scenario.

> W5: Theoretical Interaction of Spatial and Temporal Modules

We thank the reviewer for this comment. While our validation is primarily empirical, the interaction between the two modules is grounded in the fact that they address orthogonal dimensions of token utility: __intrinsic quality__ and __temporal novelty__.

The theoretical characterization of their synergy is as follows:

- __Spatial saliency (Intrinsic quality)__: Uses the L2 norm to identify tokens containing strong semantic features. This ensures that the cache retains meaningful content rather than noise.

- Temporal redundancy (Temporal novelty): Uses subspace projection to determine if a token's information is already spanned by the current frame. This ensures that the cache retains unique content rather than duplicates.

Therefore, the modules do not merely add up; they filter sequentially to maximize the unique information density of the cache. A token must be both intrinsically important (Spatial) AND not currently visible (Temporal) to be preserved. This maximizes the effective context window within a fixed budget, explaining the synergistic gains observed in Figure 4 (new Figure 5).


> Q1: Sensitivity of $r$ 

We thank the reviewer for this question. We had already investigated this exact question in Appendix B.2 and reported the results in Table 4. Our empirical results demonstrate that GUI-KV is remarkably robust to the choice of rank $r$. As shown in Table 4, varying $r$ from 8 to 128 yields consistently strong performance, with all settings outperforming the baselines reported in Table 12. While we found $r=32$ to be the optimal sweet spot, even a very low rank ($r=8$) maintains high accuracy (e.g., 21.7 at 80% budget). Regarding the suggestion of an adaptive $r$ per layer: While theoretically interesting, we believe it is practically unnecessary due to the negligible cost of the operation. As detailed in Table 3 (Appendix B.1), the QR decomposition accounts for only ~0.28% of the attention scoring compute cost (0.013 GFLOPs vs 4.607 GFLOPs). Since the computational overhead is already vanishingly small with a fixed $r$, introducing an adaptive mechanism would add implementation complexity without yielding meaningful efficiency gains.

> Q2: Formal Characterization

We thank the reviewer for the question. As we responded to W3, we would like to clarify that our "uniform budget" finding is not presented as a general mathematical theorem derived from first principles, but rather as a strong __empirical discovery specific to the GUI domains__. As detailed in Section 2.3, the condition under which this strategy holds is the presence of uniformly high attention sparsity ($>0.99$) across layers. This condition is a direct consequence of the unique visual nature of GUIs (e.g., large solid-color backgrounds, static elements), which differs fundamentally from natural scenes. Regarding the adaptation to multimodal domains with variable sparsity such as video: We acknowledge that if the input distribution shifts to include data with variable sparsity, the condition of uniform sparsity would likely break. In such scenarios, the uniform budget strategy might indeed become suboptimal. However, the __explicit scope of this paper is optimized efficiency for GUI agents__. Our contribution is identifying that for these specific tasks, the complexity of adaptive methods is unnecessary. By leveraging the specific "condition" of GUI sparsity, we can achieve state-of-the-art performance with a simpler, more efficient approach.

We thank the reviewer for their insightful assessment and for recognizing the strength of our core argument derived from the observation that GUI attention sparsity is uniformly high across all layers. We are glad that the reviewer valued how this finding leads to a clean, theory-backed conclusion that overturns prior assumptions regarding budget allocation in GUI workloads. Furthermore, we appreciate the recognition that our proposed saliency and redundancy scoring effectively ties practical algorithmic components to theoretical motivation while offering an easy-to-implement, plug-and-play solution.

> W1: Scope of the Method and Generalization to Non-GUI Domains

The reviewer is correct that this property is specific to GUI screenshots and may not hold for natural scenes or video. However, we would like to respectfully clarify that __the explicit scope of this paper is GUI agents__, as reflected in our title, our abstract, and our problem definition in Section 2.1 (new Section 3.1).
One of our contributions is precisely to identify and exploit this domain-specific characteristic (uniform high sparsity) to design a specialized, highly efficient method for GUI automation. We argue that general-purpose methods (e.g., PyramidKV) often underperform on GUIs precisely because they are designed for the varying sparsity of natural images. Conversely, __we do not claim that GUI-KV is a universal compression method for all multimodal tasks__. If applied to a domain where this uniformity breaks down (e.g., natural video understanding), the uniform budget assumption would likely be suboptimal, and one would revert to general-purpose baselines.
By narrowing our scope to the specific but critical domain of GUI agents, we are able to unlock performance and efficiency gains that generic methods cannot achieve.

> W2: Computational Overhead and Scalability of QR Decomposition

We refer the reviewer to Table 3 in Appendix B.1, which details the GFLOPs breakdown. The QR decomposition consumes only 0.013 GFLOPs, which is a negligible fraction (~0.28%) of the standard attention scoring cost (4.607 GFLOPs). Empirically, this results in a wall-clock latency increase of less than 0.1 seconds per response on AgentNetBench compared to SnapKV, confirming that the overhead is trivial in practice. Thus, the overhead remains negligible even deploying GUI-KV into real-world agents.


> W3: Theoretical Rigor of Uniform Budget Allocation

We thank the reviewer for this comment. We would like to clarify that we do not claim to provide a formal mathematical proof or a convergence guarantee for the optimality of uniform budget allocation. Our argument is grounded in empirical statistics and domain-specific analysis rather than a derived theorem.

The core logic of our approach is identifying the underlying distribution of the data. As shown in Figure 1 , the attention sparsity in GUI agents is uniformly high (>0.99) and flat across all transformer layers. Statistically, when the underlying importance distribution is uniform across layers, applying a skewed budget allocation (such as the heavy-start, light-end structure of PyramidKV) introduces a harmful inductive bias that misallocates resources.

Therefore, our claim is that uniform allocation is the empirically appropriate strategy for this specific distribution, a conclusion strongly supported by the performance comparison in Figure 2 where uniform allocation (e.g., SnapKV) outperforms complex schedules . We will revise the text to ensure we do not imply a "theorem-like" rigor, but rather a strong design choice motivated by the unique statistical properties of GUI workloads.


> W4: Parameter Justification ($\alpha$ and $\tau$)

We respectfully clarify that the values used in our experiments were $\alpha=2$ and $\tau=3.5$, as detailed in Appendix C1. We selected $\tau=3.5$ to soften the softmax distribution, preventing the selection from becoming overly peaky while preserving the relative ordering of feature magnitudes. We chose $\alpha=2$ to ensure the spatial saliency signal ($S$) acts as a strong guide alongside the attention probability ($A$). These values were determined via preliminary validation on the training split of ScreenSpot-V2 and were kept fixed across all benchmarks to ensure robustness.

We thank the reviewer for their constructive feedback and for recognizing that our work addresses the critical efficiency bottleneck of KV cache explosion, a key barrier to the real-world deployment of GUI agents. We are particularly glad that the reviewer valued our systematic analysis showing that GUI screenshots exhibit uniformly extreme attention sparsity, a finding that fundamentally distinguishes this domain from natural images and challenges prior adaptive budgeting strategies. Finally, we appreciate the acknowledgement of our paper's clarity and reproducibility, as providing transparent details, such as pseudocode and rigorous ablations, was a central goal of our submission.

> W1: Static Benchmark Concerns

We thank the reviewer for the point about the challenges of real-world dynamic components. We would like to respectfully clarify that our evaluation does account for this.

While it is true that many available GUI agent benchmarks are static (which is why we included several for comprehensive comparison), our experiments were not limited to them. We specifically included __OSWorld-Verified, which is a dynamic benchmark that requires the agent to interact with a live, real-time OS environment__. This benchmark directly addresses the reviewer's concern.


Furthermore, our core assumption of high temporal redundancy does hold in this dynamic environment. __Figure 3 (new Figure 4) in our paper shows an actual multi-step trajectory from this type of desktop task in OSWorld-Verified__. As can be seen, while small, critical UI elements change, the vast majority of the screenshot (the window, background, and static UI) remains identical across steps. This is precisely the kind of redundancy our temporal redundancy scoring is designed to exploit. Our strong performance on OSWorld-Verified (reported in Table 1) confirms that GUI-KV is effective in these real-world dynamic scenarios, not just on pre-recorded datasets.


> W2: Failure Modes

We thank the reviewer for raising this point. We agree that understanding whether compression leads to the loss of critical visual information is essential.

Regarding the specific concern about "premature pruning of small but critical UI elements," we believe the most rigorous answer lies in our quantitative results on the Grounding benchmarks (ScreenSpot-V2, ScreenSpot-Pro), rather than potentially idiosyncratic individual case studies.

As shown in Table 1, on ScreenSpot-V2, GUI-KV recovers 88.2% accuracy (at 20% budget) compared to the Full Cache's 88.3%. Hence, this near-identical performance serves as statistical proof that our method preserves the tokens corresponding to critical UI elements. If our spatial or temporal scoring were systematically pruning these "small but critical" regions, the visual grounding performance would exhibit a significant drop.

Therefore, while we acknowledge that individual failure cases exist, the aggregate data suggests that the primary failure mode is not the loss of critical UI elements, but rather mirrors __the inherent limitations of the base model itself__.

We were, however, encouraged that other reviewers (e.g., Reviewer q5EN, uck8) found the "Presentation: 3: good" and the "writing is clear." This suggests that while the current presentation was effective for some, we can certainly improve its accessibility.

We would like to respectfully clarify where the motivation and high-level ideas are presented, as we believe this is a core strength of the paper.

__Direct Motivation:__ The motivation is established immediately in the **Abstract** and **Introduction**. We explicitly state the core problem: GUI agents "face the inefficiency challenge" from processing "long sequences of high-resolution screenshots", which makes inference "slow, costly and memory-bound" (__line 12 and lines 40-43__).


__High-Level Idea:__ The high-level mechanism of GUI-KV is also explicitly summarized in the **Abstract** and again in the **Introduction**. We introduce the two novel techniques that form the basis of our method: (i) spatial saliency guidance to preserve important visual tokens and (ii) temporal redundancy scoring to prune redundant history. This high-level summary in Section 1  directly explains how our method works, addressing the reviewer's concern (__lines 18-22 and lines 62-71__).

We hope this clarifies the high-level problem and the high-level overview of our method. 

> W2: Interpretation of Figure 4 (new Figure 5) and Long-context distraction


We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation. You are correct that after the performance peak at 7 screenshots, GUI-KV's accuracy (at a 20% budget) declines more sharply than the 100% Full Cache baseline. This is a fair point.

However, we believe this chart still strongly supports our method's value for two reasons:

__Peak Performance__: The key result in this ablation is that GUI-KV matches the 100% Full Cache performance at its 7-screenshot peak, but does so with an 80% smaller cache. This demonstrates its high efficiency.

__Baseline Superiority__: Even as performance drops, GUI-KV remains consistently and significantly superior to the SnapKV baseline across all context lengths.

We interpret the sharper drop as a reasonable limitation: a model operating at a very low 20% budget is naturally more sensitive to the excessive noise introduced by 10+ screenshots. The fact that all methods, including the full-cache, decline after 7 screenshots confirms our core premise that this long-context distraction is a real problem.

Finally, the primary evidence for our claim that GUI-KV can reduce distraction and improve accuracy is in Table 1 AgentNetBench results. At 40% and 80% budget settings for GUI-KV both clearly outperform the Full Cache baseline, demonstrating that our targeted pruning is effective at removing "noise" when not faced with extreme context at a minimal budget.

We have revised Section 5.4 to explicitly acknowledge this limitation and clarify the different scenarios examined in Table 1 versus Figure 5.

We thank the reviewer for the encouraging feedback and for recognizing the significant importance of our systematic analysis of GUI attention patterns. We are particularly glad that the reviewer valued our discovery of uniformly high attention sparsity and its role in filling the gap for GUI-specific KV cache optimization. We also appreciate the recognition of GUI-KV’s practical value, specifically its ability to recover near-full-cache accuracy at modest budgets and achieve substantial reductions in decoding FLOPs while consistently outperforming competitive baselines.

> W1: Contribution of the Attention Analysis

We thank the reviewer for this perspective. We agree that our analysis serves as the vital foundation for GUI-KV's design. However, we respectfully maintain that this analysis is a distinct scientific contribution because it __challenges a prevailing assumption__ in the field. Existing methods like PyramidKV and VL-Cache rely on the premise that attention sparsity varies significantly across layers . Our findings prove this assumption false for GUIs, which exhibit "uniformly extreme" sparsity (>0.99) . Establishing this fundamental difference is a critical scientific discovery that prevents the community from misapplying complex, layer-varying optimization schemes to the GUI domain, offering value beyond just the design of our specific method.

> W2: Novelty of Temporal Redundancy Scoring

We thank the reviewer for this opportunity to clarify the technical novelty of our approach regarding the comparison to existing methods.
We would like to respectfully clarify that, to the best of our knowledge, __GUI-KV is the first KV cache compression method to explicitly exploit inter-frame redundancy patterns.__
Existing approaches for handling historical context typically rely on two methods: 
- __Accumulated Attention__: Selecting tokens purely based on how often they are attended to (e.g., H2O, SnapKV).
- __Semantic Similarity__: Merging or pruning tokens based on simple similarity measures (e.g., token merging methods).
In contrast, we are the first to exploit the temporal redundancy across frames. We have updated the introduction to reflect this novelty.

> W3: Placement of the Related Work Section

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We would like to note that placing Related Work at the end is a common structural choice in ICLR papers, intended to prioritize the immediate presentation of the novel empirical analysis and methodology. For example, multiple oral paper from ICLR 2025 place this section towards the end of the paper.

However, we agree with the reviewer that positioning it earlier can provide valuable context regarding the specific gaps in existing KV cache methods before the reader encounters our solution. Therefore, we have adopted the suggestion and have updated our draft to place the Related Work section to follow the Introduction.

summary.value:
This paper proposes GUI-KV—a plug-and-play KV cache compression method for GUI agents built on vision-language models (VLMs), addressing inefficiencies in processing long high-resolution screenshot sequences.

First, it reveals a key insight: unlike natural images, GUI screenshots exhibit uniformly high attention sparsity (>0.99) across all transformer layers, making uniform KV cache budget allocation across layers more effective than complex layer-varying schemes.

Then, GUI-KV integrates two novel mechanisms:
1. Spatial saliency guidance: Augments attention scores with the L2 norm of visual token hidden states to retain semantically important tokens.
2. Temporal redundancy scoring: Uses QR decomposition on the current frame’s key matrix to create a subspace, pruning redundant tokens from previous frames via projection residual analysis.


Evaluated on 6 benchmarks with 2 GUI models (UI-TARS-1.5-7B, OpenCUA-7B), GUI-KV recovers near-full-cache accuracy with 10–20% budgets, reduces decoding FLOPs by 38.9% (5-screenshot, 40% budget) with negligible prefill overhead, and outperforms baselines (SnapKV, PyramidKV, VL-Cache).

strengths.value:
1. The systematic analysis of attention patterns in GUI agent workloads and the effectiveness of KV cache budget allocation strategies—particularly the discovery of uniformly high attention sparsity across all transformer layers in GUIs—holds significant importance. It not only fills the gap in understanding GUI-specific characteristics for KV cache optimization but also provides valuable insights that contribute to the advancement of the broader GUI agent and KV cache research community.

2. The experimental results of GUI-KV are highly promising, especially its ability to recover near-full-cache accuracy with modest KV cache budgets (typically 10–20%) and even exceed full-cache performance in some scenarios. The quantitative results across six benchmarks (e.g., ScreenSpotV2, AgentNetBench) and two leading GUI agent models (UI-TARS-1.5-7B, OpenCUA-7B) effectively validate its superiority over competing baselines, while the efficiency analysis—showing substantial decoding FLOP reductions (e.g., 38.9% in the 5-screenshot, 40% budget setting) and negligible prefill overhead—further demonstrates its practical value.

weaknesses.value:
1. The core technical contribution is GUI-KV’s design. While the systematic analysis of GUI attention patterns (e.g., uniformly high sparsity across layers) is valuable for guiding GUI-KV’s uniform budget strategy, it may be better framed as a foundational insight rather than a standalone main contribution.

2. Regarding GUI-KV itself, its main innovation centers on integrating spatial saliency guidance and temporal redundancy scoring to form a complete compression pipeline. However, the novelty of this integration and its individual components could be further emphasized, as the current framing may contribute seem relatively limited. For instance, while the temporal redundancy scoring mechanism retains non-redundant tokens from earlier frames by projecting their keys onto the current frame’s key subspace, the description does not fully highlight how this approach differs from existing methods that leverage historical frame information.

3. The paper is highly readable, but its structure has room for improvement. Typically, the "Related Work" section (Section 5) should not be placed near the end of the paper. Related work serves to contextualize the GUI problem setting, highlight gaps in existing methods (e.g., suboptimal KV cache compression for GUIs), and justify the design of GUI-KV—all of which would better inform readers before presenting detailed analysis (Section 2) of current GUI agent challenges and the proposed methodology. If the related work has limited relevance to the core design or analysis, it could be relocated to supplementary materials; otherwise, positioning a comprehensive literature review prior to Section 2 would make the logical flow more coherent. 

4. The analysis section (Section 2) of the paper is relatively lengthy, which has constrained the space available for detailed descriptions of the proposed GUI-KV model. Notably, the methodology section (Section 3) dedicated to explaining GUI-KV’s design—including its spatial saliency guidance, temporal redundancy scoring, and their integration—spans only approximately one page. This imbalance gives the impression that the analysis part is emphasized more heavily than the methodology, which may raise concerns about whether the novelty and complexity of the proposed GUI-KV model are sufficiently articulated and highlighted

5. There’s no overall pipeline for your proposed GUI-KV. This pipeline is important and straightforward to let readers easily understand the main contributions and novelties of your paper. 

6. In Figure 3, the caption should not overlap the figure(check the right sub-figure).

7. In the ablation study (Figure 4), the y-axis is not explicitly labeled to clarify what it represents, leaving ambiguity about the specific performance indicator being measured for each method (e.g., GUI-KV, spatial-only guidance, temporal-only guidance, and SnapKV baseline).

Overall, the paper is well-written and readable, with a strong final performance. However, concerns remain regarding its novelty, structural organization, and lack of detailed clarifications. It is recommended that the authors revise the paper structure and expand discussions on the technical novelty and contributions of GUI-KV.
